summary: MarsPath is an interactive 3D map of Jezero crater built only with official NASA, USGS and IAU data, and KAIROS 2033, a mission simulator that turns that map into a survival guide for a hypothetical six-person crew. The map drapes NASA/JPL CTX elevation and imagery over the real relief and adds Perseverance's traverse, its sample sites, the Three Forks sample depot, Ingenuity's flights and the USGS geologic map. From HiRISE 1 m elevation we calculated slopes and a safest route that never exceeds NASA's 20° walking limit, and from Curiosity RAD measurements we estimated the crew's radiation dose day by day (1,003 mSv, 1.67 times NASA's career limit). The simulator follows a real NASA Ames Trajectory Browser trajectory (launch May 2033, 500 sols at Jezero, return September 2035) to recover the 10 sample tubes left at Three Forks. Every number shows its source and a confidence label, and an automated validation passes 17 of 17 checks. This matters because the first people on Mars will need maps that tell them where it is safe to walk, when to leave and which risks they face, and students need a trustworthy way to learn it. It is bilingual: Spanish and English.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MarsPath is a web map of Jezero crater, where Perseverance is exploring, with KAIROS 2033, a mission simulator built on top of it. The only hypothetical element is that a crew travels. Places, orbital dates, seasons, elevations, slopes and radiation all come from official sources or are calculated from them, and every derived number is labeled as such.

HOW IT WORKS

• Real 3D terrain: the NASA/JPL CTX digital elevation model (20 m) and CTX orthophoto, in the same projection as the rover's official map. Checked against 708 real Perseverance stops: 1.93 m median difference.

• Multi-mission layers you can turn on and off: Perseverance traverse and sample sites, the Three Forks sample depot, the Mars 2020 landing ellipse, Ingenuity's 72 flights, the USGS geologic map (SIM 3464) and official IAU names. Each layer opens a data sheet with its mission, resolution, official link and SHA-256 fingerprint.

• Risks: slopes calculated from the elevation and colored by NASA limits (20° walking in a suit and pressurized rover, from NASA EVA-EXP-0042; 25° for an Apollo-style rover). The safest route between six science stops is calculated on HiRISE 1 m elevation: 10.7 km, never steeper than 15°. The same route calculated on 20 m data crosses steps of up to 47.8° when seen at 2 m, which shows why resolution matters for crew safety.

• Radiation: day-by-day dose from Curiosity's RAD measurements (1.8 mSv/day in cruise, 0.67 mSv/day on the surface): 1,003 mSv for the whole mission, 1.67 times NASA's 600 mSv career limit, crossed on sol 375. It is clearly labeled as measured at Gale crater, because Perseverance does not measure ionizing radiation. It matches NASA's own estimate of about 1 Sv (PIA17601).

• KAIROS 2033 simulator: a real NASA Ames Trajectory Browser trajectory (launch 3 May 2033, landing 9 November 2033, 500 sols at Jezero, liftoff 19 sols before the next dust season, return 30 September 2035). Seasons come from NASA's Mars24 algorithm. The crew of six (NASA DRA 5.0) works in pairs: two stay at the base studying samples while four drive the pressurized rover with Galilei, a hypothetical robot, to recover the 10 Three Forks sample tubes and study the delta, the ancient shoreline carbonates and Cheyava Falls. A timeline, a log, the accumulated dose and a 3D close-up view show each day.

• Validation: an automated script checks the files' fingerprints, the official sources, the elevation accuracy, the route limits, that numbers match across plan, data sheets and simulator, and that assumptions are labeled. Result: 17 of 17 checks passed, shown on the cover.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It is an educational and demonstration tool, a study guide for preparing a crewed mission to Mars; it does not replace NASA operational planning. It teaches how to read Mars as a place: where it is safe to walk, why the season decides when to leave, and how much radiation a crew would get. Students and teachers can check every claim through its source, and the method (official data + derived calculations + confidence labels) works for other landing sites.

TOOLS

JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL 3D), Vite, GSAP and Motion for animation, Pretext for text layout. Python with rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy, scikit-image and Pillow for the data pipeline (download with SHA-256 log, reprojection, slopes, routes, radiation). Hosted on Vercel. Bilingual interface (Spanish / English, chosen from the browser language).

CREATIVITY

The map and the mission are one story: the team chose the name KAIROS (the Greek god of the right moment) because the mission catches the 2033 launch window and leaves Mars before the dust season. The crew, the robot Galilei and the 3D models of the base, the astronauts and the robot are the team's own design and are labeled as such.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Never inventing data: missing values (walking slope limit for Mars, rover speed, suit endurance, Jezero's own radiation) are shown as “pending” instead of estimated. Keeping Jezero (Perseverance) and Gale (Curiosity) data separate. Labeling the NASA slope limits as lunar (Artemis) references. Dust-season timing for landing and liftoff. Map resolution versus human scale. Accessibility (keyboard, reduced motion), phones, and Spanish + English.
